recognitions.title: This week, three separate claims of having fixed something didn't survive a single news cycle
recognitions.explanation: Across information warfare, energy diplomacy and debt management, the same pattern showed up: an announcement of control or resolution, followed within about a day by the other side, or the market, contradicting it. Iran claimed a sea mine sank a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz; the US called it a lie within the same cycle. A "finalized" draft deal to reopen Hormuz still contains the one unresolved question it was supposed to settle. The Fed raised rates to signal it had inflation under control, and the bond market answered by pushing yields to an 18-year high. The pattern isn't that these claims are false when made - it's that none of them are built to survive contact with the next news cycle.

evidence.text: A third tanker in two days was hit near the strait - still unclaimed, still unexplained - while Pezeshkian used it to rule out US talks entirely: "every time we come to the table, war is immediately imposed on us."

Iran says the strait is "under control of the Islamic Republic - we will not back down" - while IMF PortWatch recorded a single transit on Sept 27 against an 85-a-day prewar baseline. Control over an empty waterway is a strange thing to insist on.

The market's own conviction didn't survive a week: October hike odds were a near coin-flip on Sept 29 (50.9/49.1) and have collapsed to 21.6% today - on data the Fed itself hadn't even finished digesting when it signaled more tightening.

Federal forces say they've seized Mekelle outright - but TPLF says its own withdrawal was tactical, not defeat, fighters relocated "to reduce risks to civilians." Same event, two claims, and neither one survives contact with the other.

recognitions.title: Three things that looked like resolutions this week all deferred the real question to later
recognitions.explanation: A ceasefire, a court ruling, and a shipping framework all landed this week wearing the shape of a resolution — and in each case, the people closest to it said out loud that the actual question is still open. A peace roadmap got its first verification mission, not a verified peace. A Supreme Court stay resolved a procedural fight while its own justices noted the underlying legality is untouched. A transit deal is 'in principle' and 'still being finalized.' Each is a real step. None of them is the thing a headline would make it sound like.

evidence.text: M23 declared the outbreak over in its territory in June. It instead became the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record - hitting 1,000 cases in 40 days, versus 235 days for the 2018 DRC outbreak. A declaration, overtaken by reality at six times the speed.

The summit did produce a real $30B tariff-reduction deal and new AI-safety talks - but Trump is simultaneously slowing aircraft-part exports to China for negotiating leverage. The deal is real; so is the squeeze sitting right next to it.

Milei's minister still calls the poverty jump "far below" past levels - but disapproval among lower-income voters has surged to nearly 70%, up from 57% a year ago. The spin held for a news cycle; the voters it was aimed at didn't buy it.

Yanbu's loadings recovered after the Oct 1 strike - but the 'resolution' pattern just repeated elsewhere: the Houthis claimed a fresh strike on an Aramco facility, this time in Riyadh itself, and the Saudi-led coalition called the claim outright 'misleading.' Same dispute, new location.
